title: Know before you optimize: Diagnose Lakehouse table health with a T-SQL stored procedure
summary: A Fabric Updates Blog post introducing sp_get_table_health_metrics, a built-in stored procedure exposed through the SQL analytics endpoint that lets users diagnose the physical health of a Lakehouse Delta table in T-SQL, without opening a Spark notebook. It explains what the anomaly and storage metrics mean, and shows a check-then-act pipeline pattern that runs OPTIMIZE only when the procedure flags a real problem.
audience: Data engineers and analytics engineers who serve Lakehouse tables through the SQL analytics endpoint and want a lighter-weight way to decide when table maintenance (OPTIMIZE/compaction) is actually needed.
why_it_matters: Blind, schedule-based OPTIMIZE runs waste capacity units on healthy tables while leaving genuinely degraded tables unaddressed; a T-SQL-native diagnostic closes that gap for teams whose primary interface is the SQL analytics endpoint rather than Spark, directly informing Lakehouse operational/performance guidance.
takeaways: sp_get_table_health_metrics is a built-in stored procedure available through the Fabric SQL analytics endpoint for diagnosing Lakehouse table physical health in T-SQL.
It surfaces anomaly types like excessive small files, excessive deleted rows, missing recent checkpoints, and invalid file statistics.
It returns file-size and row-count distribution histograms so fragmentation is visible at a glance.
The recommended pattern is check-then-act: run the procedure first, and only trigger a Spark OPTIMIZE job when an anomaly is actually detected.
The SQL analytics endpoint remains read-only and cannot perform the OPTIMIZE itself; the procedure only exposes the diagnostic signal, and the fix still runs in Spark or the Lakehouse engine.

claims.text: sp_get_table_health_metrics is a built-in stored procedure exposed through the Fabric SQL analytics endpoint that provides a T-SQL-native way to check the structural/physical health of Lakehouse Delta tables.

Delta table files can drift into a suboptimal physical layout over time even when the logical data hasn't changed, which is described as the underlying cause of gradually slowing queries against Lakehouse tables.

sp_get_table_health_metrics returns anomaly-detection columns (PotentialAnomalyType and PotentialAnomalyDescription) flagging conditions such as too many small files, too many deleted rows, no recent checkpoint, or invalid file statistics, with a numeric type code for programmatic use.
The procedure's output includes snapshot and checkpoint version information used to judge whether a new Delta checkpoint is warranted.
The procedure reports file-size distribution across bins from 1 KiB to over 16 GiB and row-count distribution, letting a user spot small-file problems and data fragmentation at a glance.

Running OPTIMIZE (Spark table compaction) on a fixed schedule regardless of actual table condition is called out as an antipattern: it wastes compute/capacity units on already-healthy tables while tables that truly need attention can still be missed.

A recommended check-then-act pipeline pattern runs sp_get_table_health_metrics first inside an ETL/ELT pipeline, then conditionally triggers a Spark notebook to run OPTIMIZE only if an anomaly was detected, implementable as a two-activity Fabric pipeline with an if-condition.

Because the SQL analytics endpoint is read-only, it cannot perform table maintenance itself; sp_get_table_health_metrics only exposes the diagnostic signal, while the actual OPTIMIZE/compaction fix must still run through Spark or the Lakehouse engine.
sp_get_table_health_metrics is callable as standard T-SQL from Fabric pipelines, Azure Data Factory, dbt, or any SQL-based orchestration tool, since it does not require a Spark session to invoke.
